zone: Hozomeen and the north end of Ross Lake
_areas_note: Hozomeen Mountain alone. Verified as its own approach rather than folded into the Ross Lake corridor file: everything in that file is reached from the Highway 20 side between Newhalem and the Ross Dam trailhead, while Hozomeen sits roughly thirty miles north up the lake at the international border and is reached either by a long gravel road down from British Columbia or by boat the full length of Ross Lake. None of the Highway 20 camps serve it and no road connects the two ends of the lake on the American side. Also NOT merged into the Northern Pickets file: that zone works from Big Beaver and Little Beaver on the west shore, a different drainage and a different set of designated camps. The camps here are the Hozomeen roadhead, the two lake camps on the trail behind it, and the improvised high ground between the peaks.

sites.name: Hozomeen Campground, north end of Ross Lake
sites.capacity: Around 75 sites across two loops, all first-come and first-served with no reservations taken. The Upper Loop has been closed for hazard trees, which removes a good share of that number and also happens to be where the lake trail starts, so check what is actually open before counting on a spot.
sites.water: Seasonal potable water is provided while the campground is staffed. Outside that window, and any time the system is off, the lake and the creeks are the supply and need treating.
sites.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No fee and no reservation for the campground itself, and no backcountry permit to sleep here — but one is required the moment you walk in to the lake camps or up onto the mountain. THE BORDER IS THE COMPLICATION. The only road access is a long gravel road running south from the Trans-Canada Highway near Hope, British Columbia, and it crosses into the United States at a point with no staffed port of entry. The gate on the American side has been closed to vehicle traffic from Canada for several years, and at times foot traffic across the line has been prohibited as well. A party driving down from Canada is entering the United States, so it needs the documents for that regardless of whether anyone is there to check; the practical position has been that you cannot legally drive through, and that a normal port of entry plus the boat is the way in. Confirm the current gate status with the park and with the border agency before committing to the road, because the answer has changed more than once.
sites.notes: This is the roadhead for every route on the mountain and the only developed camping anywhere near it. It sits in deep forest on flat ground by the lake, with vault toilets, boat ramps and no trash service, so everything you bring comes out with you. There is no cell coverage and the nearest supplies are hours away in either country. The season runs roughly late May into October, bounded at the front by snow on the gravel road and at the back by the road being left unmaintained. The other way in is by water: a boat from the resort at the south end will run parties the length of the lake, taking up to six people with packs on a chartered trip that is booked and paid in advance. That is expensive and inflexible but it does not involve a border at all, which through several recent seasons has made it the only way anybody got here. In summer 2026 a lightning fire on the border grew to many thousands of acres immediately east of the mountain, crossed into Canada, and closed the entire Hozomeen area including the docks, the campground and the lake north of Silver Creek. Treat access to this peak as something to verify from scratch each season rather than as a fixed thing.

sites.name: Hozomeen Lake camp
sites.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, a few sites with a privy and food storage. Sites are assigned by night on the permit, so a walk-up can be turned away if the nights you want are taken.
sites.water: The lake is right there and is the supply. It is standing water in a shallow forested basin, so filter or treat rather than drinking it as found.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, obtained at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing system. A SEASONAL CLOSURE APPLIES: the lake is closed to entry and to camping from the first of April through the end of May to protect nesting loons, which rules out the early-season window entirely. Fires and food storage are governed by the permit; a canister is the sensible choice here whatever the minimum requirement says.
sites.notes: Something under four miles in from the campground's upper loop on an established trail, this is the obvious first night for anyone who wants to start the climb from higher than the road. It is a genuinely pleasant forested lake sitting directly beneath the mountain, and it is the better of the two lake camps by some distance. The climbing route leaves from here: parties work around the eastern shore and then angle up into the basin between the peaks, and that is where the day stops being a hike. Expect heavy deadfall and thick brush from the moment you leave the trail. The loon closure and the fire closures between them have shut this camp for large parts of recent seasons, so confirm it is open before building an itinerary on it.

sites.name: Willow Lake camp
sites.capacity: Small designated camp reached by a short spur off the main trail to the west end of the lake. A handful of sites, assigned by night.
sites.water: The lake, which is a long shallow marshy basin rather than clear open water. Treat it, and expect to walk a little to find a spot worth drawing from.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same system as the rest of the east shore. No advance reservation for most nights here; plan on the walk-up allocation and carry a fallback night in mind.
sites.notes: Roughly two trail miles south of the junction for Hozomeen Lake, on the long north-south trail that runs the entire east shore of Ross Lake. It matters to this peak mainly as an overflow and as the link to the alternative approach: a party that cannot get to the north end at all can walk in from the Highway 20 end of that trail instead, which is a multi-day proposition but does not depend on a border gate or a chartered boat. The lake itself is marshy and buggy through midsummer and is a worse camp than Hozomeen Lake, so take it only if the better one is full. Both camps sit low in dense forest with no view of the climbing.

sites.name: Improvised bivouacs in the western basin between the peaks
sites.capacity: No established site and no site count. Parties have reported scratching out a few rough platforms among scattered boulders on a steep forested slope, enough for one small party sleeping poorly. THERE IS NO CAMP HERE — this is where people stop because they have run out of daylight, not somewhere anyone chose.
sites.water: This is the hard part and worth planning around. The one stream in the basin runs in a channel that deepens into a slot as you climb, and parties have found it reachable at a single awkward spot at around four thousand feet and nowhere above that. Fill everything you are carrying when you can get to water, because you may not get another chance before the ground goes flat enough to sleep on.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Hozomeen cross-country zone, which allows a maximum party of six and a maximum of three parties on any night. It is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one, so the permit is collected in person, in practice at Marblemount. Cross-country camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight of both, and only on snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadow and never within a hundred feet of water. NO FIRES in the zone. Waste goes in a cathole, or is carried out where the ground will not take one.
sites.notes: The mountain is two rock summits above a basin, and the approach to that basin from the lake is the crux of the whole trip for most parties: a slow grind through blowdown and heavy brush with no path, on which fifteen miles and seven thousand feet of gain and loss is a fair reckoning for the round trip. Strong parties do go car to car, and several accounts describe that decision being regretted around hour twelve. Sleeping up here shortens the summit day considerably, at the cost of hauling water up a slope with almost none on it and sleeping on ground that is not flat. There is a second line from the road along the cleared border swath running east from near the ranger station, which is shorter and is described by people who have used it as more unpleasant than the lake approach rather than less. Both are late-summer propositions: snow lingers in the basin, and the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
